text:
Short answer: no, not on its own. An all-female panel of four is not evidence of anything, and if you lead with it you will damage your position rather than strengthen it.

**Why panel composition is weak evidence**

Newsroom management and HR both skew female in most public broadcasters, so a four-person panel landing all-women is unremarkable — it's the kind of thing that happens by chance fairly often. More to the point, a useful self-check: if the panel had been four men and a man had got the job, would you read anything into it? Most people wouldn't. Single-sex panels in the other direction have been routine for decades and nobody treated them as proof of a rigged process.

The one narrow version of this worth holding onto: many public bodies have their own recruitment policy stating panels should be mixed where practicable. If your employer has such a policy and breached it, that's a legitimate *procedural* point — a box they failed to tick. It is not proof of bias, and it only matters as a supporting detail if something substantive went wrong. Worth checking the policy quietly; not worth building a case on.

**Where the real question is**

"Strong experience of digital media." That line is the thing to focus on, and there are two possibilities.

If digital capability was an essential criterion in the published job description and person specification, then the panel was entitled — obliged, really — to weigh it heavily, and eight years with strong digital beats fifteen without it. Length of service and being the incumbent deputy don't entitle you to the step up. Organisations quite often promote past an internal deputy precisely because they want a change of direction, and the deputy reads it as a slight when it was a strategic choice.

If digital was absent from the criteria, or listed as desirable rather than essential, and it has suddenly become the headline justification — that's a much more interesting problem. It suggests the criteria may have moved during the process, which is a real procedural failure and one that tribunals and internal appeals actually care about.

So: dig out the original job advert, job description and person spec. Compare them to the announcement. That comparison will tell you more than speculating about the panel ever will. Also bear in mind the announcement is PR copy written to sell the appointment, not a reasoned decision — don't over-read a single phrase in it.

**The silence is your actual live issue**

Two weeks with no response to a reasonable request is the thing to push on now, and it's the one place you're clearly in the right. Send a short, dry follow-up to whoever ran the process, copying HR:

- reference your original request and its date
- ask specifically for your interview scores against each criterion, the panel's notes, and the reasons you were not appointed
- ask when you can expect a response
- no theories, no grievance framing, no mention of the panel

Keep it to five lines. The flat, procedural tone is what gets answered. If you're in a jurisdiction with data protection rights — the UK, EU, and most of Europe — you also have a right to the personal data held about you, which typically covers interview notes and scoresheets, and that request carries a statutory deadline. That's a stronger lever than a polite ask, though it's also a visible escalation, so hold it in reserve.

**Two things to be aware of**

Time limits for formal complaints are often short and unforgiving — in the UK, discrimination claims are generally three months less a day from the act complained of. I don't know where you are, so check your jurisdiction and your internal appeal window now rather than after you've got the feedback. Don't let the clock run out while you wait for an email.

And the career calculus. You presumably still work there, which means the woman who got the job is now your boss. Raising a gender discrimination concern on this evidence would be visible, probably unsuccessful, and very hard to come back from. A procedural complaint about criteria and feedback is survivable and may even be respected. A complaint about the panel's sex is not.

My honest read: the gender theory is also likely to distort how you receive the feedback when it finally arrives. Get the documents and the scores first. If there's something wrong with this process, that's where it will be visible.
